stem: An employee is being terminated for cause. Regarding their system access, what should happen FIRST?

options.text: Revoke/disable their access immediately, coordinated with the termination
options.rationale: For-cause terminations require immediate access revocation to prevent retaliatory misuse of still-active accounts.

options.text: Leave access active for two weeks as a courtesy
options.rationale: Leaving a for-cause terminee's access active invites sabotage or data theft.

options.text: Wait for the next quarterly access review
options.rationale: Delaying revocation to a periodic review leaves a dangerous open window.

options.text: Announce the termination company-wide before revoking access
options.rationale: Publicizing before revoking gives the individual time and motive to misuse active accounts.

stem: An employee who changed departments three times retains access from every prior role. This accumulation is MOST accurately called what?

options.rationale: Retaining access across role changes accumulates unnecessary rights — privilege creep — violating least privilege.
This is the opposite of least privilege; the user holds excess access.
Separation of duties splits tasks; it does not describe accumulated access.
Deprovisioning removes access; here access was never removed, causing creep.

stem: An audit finds an active account belonging to an employee who left the company six months ago. This is MOST accurately which risk?

options.text: An orphaned account, a serious unmanaged access risk
options.rationale: An active account of a departed user is an orphaned account — a common breach vector that should have been deprovisioned.
A departed user's active account is improperly retained, not properly provisioned.
Leaving a departed user's account active is a failure, not a least-privilege success.
This is unrelated to separation of duties.

stem: An employee transfers from finance to HR. To uphold least privilege, what should happen FIRST regarding their access?

options.text: Review and remove access no longer needed for the new role before/while granting new access
options.rationale: On a mover event, obsolete access should be reviewed and revoked to prevent privilege creep as new role access is provisioned.

options.text: Keep all finance access and add HR access
options.rationale: Retaining old access while adding new causes privilege creep.

options.text: Do nothing since they are still an employee
options.rationale: A role change requires an access review; inaction leaves inappropriate access.

options.text: Delete the account entirely and never restore access
options.rationale: The user still needs role-appropriate HR access; removing everything blocks their work.

stem: To ensure users' entitlements remain appropriate over time, what ongoing control is BEST?

options.text: Periodic access reviews/recertification with manager attestation
options.rationale: Recertification periodically re-validates that each user's access is still warranted, catching drift and stale entitlements.

options.text: Granting access once and never reviewing it
options.rationale: One-time provisioning without review lets entitlements drift out of alignment.

options.text: Letting users approve their own access
options.rationale: Self-approval undermines oversight and least privilege.
Disabling logging reduces visibility and does not review entitlements.

stem: Which system is MOST commonly the authoritative source that should trigger automated provisioning and deprovisioning?

options.rationale: HR typically records hires, transfers, and terminations, making it the authoritative trigger for identity lifecycle changes.
This has no role in identity provisioning.
A marketing site does not record employment status changes.
A personal calendar is not an authoritative HR source.

stem: To onboard a new hire quickly, an admin copies all permissions from an existing senior employee. What is the MOST significant risk?

options.text: The new hire inherits excessive privileges, violating least privilege
options.rationale: Access cloning propagates the senior user's broad (possibly excessive) rights to the new hire, over-provisioning them.

options.text: The new hire gets too little access
options.rationale: Cloning a senior user typically over-grants, not under-grants, access.
Cloning permissions does not implement MAC; it copies existing rights.
Cloning undermines least privilege by spreading excess access.

stem: A company repeatedly forgets to disable accounts when employees leave. What is the BEST systemic fix?

options.text: Automate deprovisioning by linking identity management to the HR system so departures trigger account disablement
options.rationale: Automated, HR-triggered deprovisioning removes reliance on manual memory, promptly disabling departed users' accounts.
Relying on memory is what caused the recurring failure.
Never disabling accounts maximizes orphaned-account risk.
Removing the authoritative source would worsen, not fix, lifecycle management.

stem: When provisioning a new user, which approach BEST aligns with security best practice?

options.text: Grant only the minimum role-appropriate access needed for the job
options.rationale: Least-privilege provisioning limits exposure if the account is compromised and avoids over-granting.

options.text: Grant broad access up front to avoid future requests
options.rationale: Pre-granting broad access violates least privilege and increases risk.

options.text: Give every new user administrator rights
options.rationale: Universal admin rights are a severe least-privilege violation.
Access cloning spreads potentially excessive privileges.

stem: The 'Joiner–Mover–Leaver' model describes which of the following?

options.text: The stages of the identity/access provisioning lifecycle
options.rationale: JML captures onboarding (joiner), role change (mover), and offboarding (leaver) in the access lifecycle.
JML is an identity lifecycle concept, not a routing protocol.
JML has nothing to do with fire suppression.
JML is not a cryptographic algorithm.

stem: An audit reveals widespread privilege creep from unremoved access after transfers. What is the BEST corrective control going forward?

options.text: Enforce access review on every role change and periodic recertification to remove stale access
options.rationale: Reviewing/removing access at each mover event plus periodic recertification systematically prevents and cleans up privilege creep.

options.text: Grant even more access to simplify things
options.rationale: Adding access worsens privilege creep.
Freezing roles is impractical and does not address the process gap.
Disabling all accounts halts the business and is not a targeted fix.

stem: An employee gives two weeks' notice and departs on good terms. What is the BEST deprovisioning practice on their last day?

options.text: Disable/revoke all their access and recover assets at the end of their final day per the offboarding process
options.rationale: Even amicable departures require prompt, complete access revocation and asset recovery at separation to avoid orphaned access.
Leaving accounts active creates orphaned-account risk.

options.text: Only remove their email and nothing else
options.rationale: Partial revocation leaves exploitable residual access.

options.text: Escalate their privileges as a farewell gift
options.rationale: Increasing a departing user's access is reckless.

stem: During access recertification, who is MOST appropriate to attest that a user's access is still needed?

options.rationale: Managers or data owners know the user's job needs and are appropriate attesters for whether access remains warranted.
Someone without knowledge of the user's role cannot meaningfully attest.

options.text: The user themselves with no oversight
options.rationale: Self-attestation without oversight undermines the control.
Customers have no basis to attest to internal access needs.

stem: Which activity is BEST for detecting orphaned or inappropriate accounts?

options.text: Periodic account/entitlement reviews reconciled against the HR authoritative source
options.rationale: Reconciling accounts against the HR record surfaces orphaned accounts and entitlements that no longer match employment status.

options.text: Assuming all accounts are valid forever
options.rationale: Assuming validity lets orphaned accounts persist undetected.
Removing logs reduces the ability to detect issues.
This increases risk and does nothing to detect orphaned accounts.

stem: In identity management, 'deprovisioning' refers to which of the following?

options.text: Revoking access and disabling accounts when a user no longer needs them
options.rationale: Deprovisioning removes access/disables accounts at role change or departure.
That describes provisioning, not deprovisioning.
Encryption is a separate control, not deprovisioning.
That is privilege escalation/expansion, the opposite of deprovisioning.

stem: A team uses one shared login for a critical system. From a lifecycle/accountability view, what is the MOST significant problem?

options.text: Actions cannot be attributed to individuals, and the account is hard to deprovision when one member leaves
options.rationale: Shared accounts destroy individual accountability and complicate the leaver process, since a departing member's access can't be cleanly removed without disrupting others.
Shared accounts typically over-grant and undermine least privilege.
Shared accounts reduce, not improve, audit attribution.
Shared accounts have clear accountability and lifecycle downsides.

stem: A contractor's engagement ends. Regarding their system access, what should happen FIRST?

options.text: Revoke the contractor's access and disable their accounts at engagement end
options.rationale: Contractor access should be promptly revoked at the end of engagement, just like employee offboarding, to avoid lingering access.

options.text: Leave the contractor's credentials active for future convenience
options.rationale: Retaining former-contractor access is an unmanaged risk.

options.text: Promote the contractor to full admin
options.rationale: Elevating a departing contractor is reckless.

options.text: Do nothing since they were never an employee
options.rationale: Contractors still have access that must be revoked at engagement end.

stem: Why is the timeliness of deprovisioning MOST important from a security standpoint?

options.text: Delays leave active credentials that departed or reassigned users (or attackers who obtain them) can misuse
options.rationale: The longer access remains after it is no longer warranted, the larger the window for misuse by the former holder or an attacker.
Deprovisioning timeliness is about risk, not network performance.
Deprovisioning is unrelated to cryptographic strength.
Timely revocation directly reduces the exposure window, a real security impact.

stem: For highly privileged administrator accounts, which lifecycle practice is MOST important?

options.text: Tighter provisioning, more frequent recertification, and prompt revocation given their elevated risk
options.rationale: Privileged accounts carry high risk, so they warrant stricter provisioning, more frequent review, and immediate revocation when no longer needed.

options.text: Looser controls since admins are trusted
options.rationale: Elevated privilege demands tighter, not looser, lifecycle controls.
High-risk accounts especially require regular review.
Sharing privileged accounts destroys accountability and increases risk.

stem: Which factor is LEAST relevant to managing the access provisioning lifecycle?

options.rationale: An employee's lunch preference has no bearing on provisioning, review, or deprovisioning, making it least relevant.
Prompt revocation is central to the lifecycle.

options.text: Removing old access on role change
options.rationale: Removing stale access prevents privilege creep, a key lifecycle activity.
Recertification keeps entitlements appropriate over time.
